title: History of the Trail of Tears, Part II
summary: Part two of the Trail of Tears history. Picks up after the 1830 Indian Removal Act: the Choctaw are removed first and the term "Trail of Tears" is coined by a Choctaw chief's description; the Chickasaw are moved; the Second Seminole War (1835-1842) and Third Seminole War (1855-1858) are covered. The Cherokee are split by the secret Treaty of New Echota, led by the Treaty Party (John Ridge, Major Ridge, Elias Boudinot, Stand Watie), against the wishes of Chief John Ross and most of the Cherokee Nation. Federal troops under General Winfield Scott forcibly removed the Cherokee in 1838 and held them in stockades; thousands died on the march west, including Ross's wife. Impacts on towns along the route, the African American slave trade expansion tied to cotton land, the 1839 assassinations of Treaty Party leaders, the Civil War divide, the 2009 federal apology, and Georgia's Cherokee rose. Ends with a listener mail correction about the Holy Roman Empire.

segments.title: Opening and recap of part one
segments.summary: Hosts introduce part two and recap the 1830 Indian Removal Act and the pressure on eastern tribes to leave their land.

segments.title: Choctaw removal and the origin of the term Trail of Tears
segments.summary: The Choctaw are the first tribe removed under the treaty process, carried out by the War Department. Thousands die in three waves of migration. A Choctaw chief describes the journey as a trail of tears and death upon arrival in Oklahoma, the origin of the name.

segments.title: Why removal worsened: encroachment and loss of European allies
segments.summary: Removal continued despite the publicity. The War Department failed to protect tribes from white encroachment in the west, and after the War of 1812 and the Seminole Wars, no European power remained to act as a buffer or ally for the Indians.

segments.title: Georgia land lotteries and the Chickasaw removal
segments.summary: Georgia's Cherokee land lotteries between 1805 and 1832 gave white men chances at land that was not theirs. The Chickasaw then agreed to move, only to find they had no land in Indian Territory and had to buy land from the Choctaw.

segments.title: Seminole Wars
segments.summary: Andrew Jackson's First Seminole War did not defeat the Seminoles. The Second Seminole War (1835-1842) was a long conflict after a small faction secretly negotiated removal, costing thousands of lives and about a billion dollars. The Third Seminole War (1855-1858) was the last attempt at removal, and the holdouts were eventually paid for their land.

segments.title: Treaty of New Echota and the Treaty Party
segments.summary: About twenty Cherokee leaders, the Treaty Party, including John Ridge, Major Ridge, Elias Boudinot and Stand Watie, secretly negotiated the Treaty of New Echota giving up Cherokee land. Chief John Ross, backed by the Cherokee Council, negotiated separately for a higher price and citizenship. About 17,000 Cherokee signed a petition against the treaty, but the Senate ratified it.

segments.title: Forced removal of the Cherokee in 1838
segments.summary: After the three-year deadline, only about 2,000 of 18,000 Cherokee had left. President Martin Van Buren sent General Winfield Scott with about 7,000 troops. The Cherokee were forced from their homes at gunpoint in 1838 and held in thirty-one stockade posts, where many died of exposure, hunger and disease.

segments.title: The westward march, deaths, and the assassinations
segments.summary: Cherokee walked west, barefoot in many cases, with wagons for the elderly and young and some traveling by steamship. Many thousands died on the march, and a soldier's account describes the deaths. Chief John Ross later oversaw the final migrations. In June 1839 Ross's supporters assassinated Major Ridge, John Ridge and Elias Boudinot; Stand Watie escaped.

segments.title: Impact on towns, slavery expansion, and legacy
segments.summary: Towns along the route saw economic booms and some exploitation through tolls, and some towns refused passage. Removal opened land for cotton, expanding the slave trade. Discussion of the Civil War divide between Treaty Party and Ross supporters, the 2009 federal apology, and Georgia's adoption of the Cherokee rose.

segments.title: Listener mail: Holy Roman Empire correction
segments.summary: A listener corrects the hosts' references to the Holy Roman Empire, explaining its origins in the ninth century from Charlemagne's Frankish kingdom and its distinction from Rome and the papal states.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners to search for more on the Trail of Tears, give social media and email contact details, and point to the website.
